item.title: Visible light drives bright extreme-ultraviolet high harmonics
item.description:
Maximilian Karst, Martin Gebhardt, Lucas Eisenbach, Philipp Gierschke, Themistoklis Sidiropoulos, Robert Klas, Jan Rothhardt, Jens Limpert
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79615-1
Abstract Coherent extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) light is a central tool in modern photon science, probing the electronic, chemical and structural properties of matter. High-harmonic generation can extend the reach of laser sources into this spectral range, but the achievable photon flux falls sharply as photon energy increases. We show experimentally and theoretically that plasma-core-induced self-guiding of a visible-wavelength driver in helium sustains high intensity and favorable phase matching over an extended propagation length. We achieve a conversion efficiency of up to 10 −6 in a single high-harmonic line and phase-matched emission extending to 100 eV. With less than 10 W of average power at 516 nm from a frequency-doubled ytterbium laser, we generate 1.8 × 10 11 photons s −1 within 2 % bandwidth at 13.5 nm (91.8 eV), exceeding previous reports by more than an order of magnitude. These results establish a power-scalable XUV platform for actinic metrology, spectroscopy and coherent imaging.

item.title: Influenza A virus orchestrates ciliated cell fate and injury during the mucociliary damage repair cycle
item.description:
Biying Xiao, Xuenan Zhao, Shiyong Guo, Mingyue Fan, Hui Zhang, Xiaojing Yang, Lulu Zhang, Yuting Li, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79726-9
Abstract Influenza A virus causes acute damage to airway epithelium, yet the damage–repair cycle and mechanisms underlying persistent mucociliary clearance (MCC) dysfunction long after viral clearance remain unclear. Here, using longitudinal in vivo quantitative micro-optical coherence tomography, we show that global MCC impairment persists for more than 14 days, marked by impaired ciliary activity and sustained mucus hypersecretion in male mice infected with the H1N1 influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (PR8) strain. Through lineage tracing and multi-omics analyses, we identify an immune-mediated transdifferentiation program in which IFN signaling activates the IDO1–AhR axis to drive ciliated-to-mucous cell fate transition and chronic muco-obstruction after H1N1 PR8 infection in a reconstructed human bronchial epithelium model. In parallel, we identify the viral M2 protein as a key driver of ciliary loss, suppressing the host TP73–FOXJ1–RFX3 regulatory axis and promoting proteasomal degradation of FOXJ1. Together, these findings uncover host- and virus-driven pathways that cooperatively impair airway epithelial homeostasis and sustain MCC failure beyond active infection, highlighting therapeutic targets for post-influenza muco-obstructive disease.

item.title: A highly distorted benzenium cation
item.description:
Baojing Tian, Jiaofan Chang, Qi Sun, Qi Zhang, Shaowen Zhang, He Huang, Xudong Xu, Zongyao Sun, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79596-1
Abstract In contrast to the well-explored peripheral functionalization of benzene, its skeletal alteration remains underdeveloped. Here, we report a highly distorted benzenium cation, 2,3-dihydroxy-1,4,6-triamino-5-nitrobenzenium (TANBC + ), featuring a ring twist angle of 35.91° and a ring C-C bond length of 1.540 Å, both rank the highest among all benzenium cations. Such pronounced structural distortions endow TANBC + with unique electronic properties, including a highly positive electrostatic charge on the warped carbon, weak aromaticity, and a low ring bond dissociation energy. Consequently, instead of undergoing peripheral functionalization like typical benzenium cations, TANBC + participates in three distinct benzene ring reconstruction pathways or remains inert under standard electrophilic substitution conditions. Moreover, despite its distorted structure, TANBC + exhibits excellent ambient stability, stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding, and can be synthesized readily without harsh conditions usually required for conventional benzenium cations. This work not only introduces a new strategy for benzene reconstruction but also redefines the role of benzenium cations from mediators of peripheral functionalization to promoters of skeletal alteration, thereby advancing the fundamental chemistry of benzene.

item.title: Deep ultraviolet gallium-oxide avalanche photodiodes reaching an impulse-response-derived gain-bandwidth record of 152 GHz
item.description:
Dianmeng Dong, Jintao Fu, Hongda Ren, Qingyi Zhang, Tao Zhang, Xingsi Liu, Yilin Cao, Min Peng, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79355-2
Abstract Solar-blind Ga 2 O 3 -based photodetectors, sensing deep ultraviolet (DUV) light (200–280 nm), offer unparalleled opportunities for secure non-line-of-sight optical communication. Yet their practical applications have been largely hindered by the relatively low gain-bandwidth product (GBP), due to the fundamental trade-off between response speed and photoelectric gain. Here, we report nanosecond-level-response solar-blind avalanche photodetectors based on β-Ga 2 O 3 /MgO/La 0.8 Ca 0.2 MnO 3 (LCMO) n-Barrier-p heterojunctions with high apparent gain over 2.6×10 6 , thereby achieving an impulse-response-derived record-breaking 152 GHz gain-bandwidth product — outpacing the state-of-the-art Ga 2 O 3 -based devices by 3 orders of magnitude. The MgO interlayer enables lattice matching and engineered conduction band offset to boost gain and suppress dark current, while the p-type LCMO layer introduces a large valence band offset and simultaneously establishes a hole-selective transport highway for ultrafast response. This work not only resolves the longstanding gain-bandwidth trade-off in DUV photodetection but also presents a universal band-engineering framework for next-generation optoelectronics.

item.title: A spectral framework for revealing the hidden low-dimensional structure in stochastic reaction networks
item.description:
Ankit Gupta, Mustafa Khammash
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79229-7
Abstract Stochastic reaction networks govern noise-driven dynamics in systems ranging from gene regulation to cellular signalling and population processes. Yet their high dimensionality and sensitivity to initial states obscure transient mechanisms and limit reliable inference from experimental data. Here, we show that stochastic reaction networks in biological systems often exhibit dominant low-dimensional spectral structure that shapes their dynamics. We develop a spectral framework based on the stochastic Koopman operator that identifies these dominant dynamical modes directly from simulated trajectories, yielding reduced representations with computable error bounds. This reduction enables accurate analytical descriptions of the time evolution of moments, parameter sensitivities, and cross-spectral densities, while achieving order-of-magnitude computational gains relative to standard simulation-based methods. Applied to synthetic gene circuits, our framework reveals the spectral organisation of stochastic oscillators, enables systematic comparison of competing intracellular controllers, and facilitates inference of initial-state distributions from single-cell snapshot population data collected over time. Together, these results establish a principled spectral description of stochastic reaction dynamics and provide a foundation for analysing and inferring high-dimensional noise-driven biological systems.

item.title: Orbital spectroscopy links dust source composition to atmospheric acidity and nitrate
item.description:
Rubén Soussé Villa, Oriol Jorba, María Gonçalves Ageitos, Jeronimo Escribano, Vincenzo Obiso, Ron L. Miller, Longlei Li, Natalie M. Mahowald, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79201-5
Abstract Mineral dust affects atmospheric chemistry, air quality, and climate, yet its impacts remain uncertain because its mineral composition is poorly constrained. Here we combine NASA EMIT orbital imaging spectroscopy with a satellite-constrained global chemistry model to quantify how source-resolved calcite variability alters aerosol chemistry and optical properties. EMIT-derived calcite improves agreement with airborne observations and reveals contrasts in dust alkalinity. Compared with globally averaged calcite, source-resolved calcite shifts regional annual mean aerosol pH by -0.6 to +0.5 units, with local changes exceeding 1 pH unit across substantial areas of the most affected dust-influenced regions, reaching -4 to +3 units in limited areas. These acidity changes reorganize secondary inorganic aerosol formation, nitrate partitioning, and extreme nitrate events, particularly where dust interacts with anthropogenic pollution. In contrast, calcite-driven secondary-aerosol radiative effects are small relative to those caused by spatial variations in iron-oxide absorption. These results show that calcite variability strongly modulates heterogeneous chemistry, whereas iron oxides dominate radiative impacts.

item.title: ER-associated biogenesis of PINK1 preprotein for neuronal mitophagy
item.description:
J. Tabitha Hees, Inmaculada Segura, Andrea Schneider, Martina Schifferer, Sultan Bekbayev, Jana Lindner, Simone Mattei, Thomas Misgeld, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79754-5
Abstract Given the large size of neurons, local maintenance of mitochondria is crucial to counteract insults to this organelle in axons and dendrites. The Parkinson-related mitochondrial kinase PINK1 plays a central role in mitochondrial quality control, which in neurons requires the transport of Pink1 mRNA by mitochondrial hitch-hiking. However, how and where PINK1 is locally translated and processed has remained unclear. Using live-cell imaging, we trace local PINK1 translation sites and preprotein dynamics, revealing a concerted interplay between mitochondria and the ER, with endolysosomes frequently localized adjacent to the site of translation. Upon metabolically regulated untethering from mitochondria, Pink1 mRNA relocates to ribosomes in proximity to the ER and endolysosomes for translation of the PINK1 preprotein. The ER chaperone DNAJB6 shields the PINK1 preprotein in transit to mitochondria, following the post-translational ER-SURF pathway. Consequently, loss of DNAJB6 leads to persistent ER/endolysosome-associated PINK1 precursor stores and failure of mitophagy upon mitochondrial damage. Our findings reveal that neuronal PINK1 protein translation switches between mitochondrially anchored co-translational and ER-associated post-translational import states, with functional implications for mitochondrial quality control.

item.title: A protein repeat interruption rule governs Nebulin stability and explains in-frame NEB mutations
item.description:
Lacramioara Fabian, Tasneem Y. Al Mudarris, Sylvia J. P. Bogaards, Senthuri Viththiyapaskaran, Esmat Karimi, Gerrie P. Farman, Xiucheng Cui, Jason Burgess, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79648-6
Abstract Nemaline myopathy is a rare congenital muscle disease associated with thin filament disruption that is currently without treatment. Biallelic mutations in Nebulin are the most common cause of nemaline myopathy. Nebulin encodes a giant protein with a primary function of establishing thin filament length. Nebulin protein has a large central region composed of a series of thin filament binding super repeats. Many Nebulin mutations are small in-frame deletions within individual super repeats. Why these deletions cause disease remains unclear. To study this, we generated a series of zebrafish lines, including ones carrying in-frame partial super repeat deletions and ones harboring complete/intact super repeat deletions. Partial super repeat deletions destabilize and reduce Nebulin protein, resulting in severe phenotypes and early death. Conversely, complete super repeat deletions preserve Nebulin stability and expression, and induce no overt phenotypes. Our work provides mechanistic insights and informs future therapeutic approaches for Nebulin-related Nemaline myopathy.
